value.overview: The Pomarine Jaeger (Stercorarius pomarinus) is the largest and most heavily built of the three jaeger species. It is a powerful seabird related to gulls and skuas, famous for chasing other birds and stealing their food. It breeds on high-Arctic tundra and spends the nonbreeding season mostly over the open ocean. Adults have distinctive twisted, spoon-shaped central tail feathers, while immature birds are variable and can be difficult to identify at sea.
value.classification: The Pomarine Jaeger belongs to the order Charadriiformes and family Stercorariidae, the skua and jaeger family. Its scientific name is Stercorarius pomarinus.
value.identification: This is a bulky, barrel-chested seabird with broad, pointed wings, a thick bill, and a powerful flight style. Adults commonly show a dark cap and breast band, extensive white flashes in the wings, and black around the base of the bill. Breeding adults have elongated, twisted, spoon-shaped central tail feathers. Color varies among light, intermediate, and dark morphs. Immature birds are usually brown and strongly barred, and careful attention to size, body shape, bill thickness, and wing pattern is needed.
value.rangeHabitat: The Pomarine Jaeger breeds across high-Arctic tundra in northern Russia, Alaska, and Arctic Canada, especially in wet low-vegetation areas where lemmings are available. Outside the breeding season it is highly pelagic, occupying offshore waters across several oceans, including the Caribbean and waters off Central and South America. In Costa Rica it occurs as an uncommon marine migrant or nonbreeding visitor, mainly offshore; records include the Pacific coast and Golfo Dulce, and it is not a regular terrestrial bird.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds move from Arctic breeding grounds to tropical and subtropical oceans after breeding. In Costa Rica, it is an irregular and generally uncommon offshore migrant or visitor, most likely encountered from boats or coastal viewpoints rather than inland.
value.breeding: Breeding is closely tied to Arctic lemming abundance, and Pomarine Jaegers may delay or skip breeding when food is scarce. Pairs nest on the ground, usually on a slight rise or hummock in wet tundra, where both adults create a shallow depression. The usual clutch is one or two eggs. Incubation lasts about 25–27 days, and the downy young can leave the nest within a few days of hatching. Both parents defend the territory and raise the young.
value.dietFeeding: During the breeding season, the diet consists mainly of brown lemmings and other small tundra rodents, with occasional shorebirds, ducks, and ptarmigan. At sea and during migration, the diet becomes more varied and includes fish, squid, crabs, insects, carrion, eggs, and seabirds. The species frequently uses kleptoparasitism, aggressively pursuing gulls, terns, petrels, shearwaters, and other seabirds until they drop or regurgitate their food.
value.behavior: Pomarine Jaegers are strong, direct fliers and are less acrobatic than the smaller Parasitic and Long-tailed Jaegers. At sea they may gather in loose groups, rest on the water, follow vessels, or investigate fishing activity and floating food. Their attacks on other seabirds rely more on size and force than prolonged aerial maneuvering. On breeding grounds they defend territories with calls, direct flights, wing-raising displays, and aggressive approaches to intruders.

conservation.populationTrend: Global population trend is not reliably established and is generally reported as unknown. Breeding success can fluctuate substantially with cyclic changes in lemming abundance.
